newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weaker yen could hurt, not help, Japan economy.
newsitem.headline: Weaker yen could hurt, not help, Japan economy.

text.p: Maybe you can have too much of a good thing.

The yen's precipitous slide to within a hair's breadth of 115 to the dollar is raising fears that a further weakening of the currency -- traditionally viewed as a plus for Japan's giant economy -- might end up doing more harm than good.

The dollar rose to 114.92 yen in early Tuesday trade in Tokyo, its highest level since April 1993, propelled by expectations that rock-bottom Japanese interest rates would keep Japanese money flowing abroad. The greenback then fell back on profit-taking.
"We are probably approaching a threshold at which some benefits of the yen's depreciation will turn negative," said Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston.

Economists said big Japanese companies no longer reaped the same benefits once generated by a weaker yen because of their push to move output offshore in recent years when the Japanese currency was scaling new heights against the dollar.

The yen soared to a post-war high of 79.75 against the dollar in April 1995. A weaker currency makes a country's exports more price-competitive abroad, while a stronger currency tarnishes their allure for foreign buyers.
"It used to be common sense that a weaker yen was a plus for Japan's economy, because exports became more profitable," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute.
"The positive impact is still there, but since exporters have moved production abroad, the benefits are much smaller."
The yen's latest slump in fact is making Japanese firms worry about the wisdom of their offshore production drive and encouraging some to shift part of that output back home.
"We've heard from the industrial sector in the last several months that more yen weakness is not a good idea," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.

"If it was cheaper for Japanese company 'XYZ' to source its U.S. market from Malaysia when the dollar was at 90 yen, that might not be true anymore at 115. So they built all these plants for nothing," Feldman said.

Honda Motor Co Ltd said last week it might move production of its popular estate model, the Accord Wagon, back to Japan from the United States, adding the possible shift was part of its policy of making products where they sell best.
The weakening yen, meanwhile, also risks sparking inflation due to costlier imports, boosting bond yields and raising the cost of funds for Japanese firms, private economists said.

"There are some beneficial effects, but overall it's probably a bad thing, because the positive effects from stimulating exports are offset by the negative effect of higher (priced) imports and the eventual effects of higher inflation on bond yields," said Feldman.
A Bank of Japan official said on Tuesday, however, that he was not particularly worried about the impact of a weaker yen on domestic prices and a government official echoed that view.
"It is true that prices of imported goods are rising. But the situation is not one that we must be worried about," Economic Planning Agency Vice Minister Shimpei Nukaya said.
Finance ministry mandarins appear still wedded to their policy of promoting a weaker yen as a way to stimulate the economy without more public spending.

But some other economic policy makers, such as officials at the trade ministry seem, seem less enthused. "It would be good if it (the dollar/yen rate) stabilised around current levels," Trade Minister Shunpei Tsukahara said.

Economists also fear that the yen's weakness will ease pressure on corporate Japan to carry out the restructuring needed to improve global competitiveness, and on policy makers to enact the deregulation needed to ensure long-term growth.
"Japan's national agenda to deregulate and enjoy international prices...goes out the window if the yen stays at current levels for an extended period," Sasaki-Smith said.
